description: Space causes bone loss and meltdowns? Sounds like Alex Uni engineering! We are "Coach b Fanella w Cap"—four guys armed with our coach, laptops, and the sheer power of a white Fanella. We’re building health-tracking software for the Space Apps Challenge. If we can survive 3 AM debugging, astronauts can definitely survive zero gravity!
summary: Astromedical, is a Healthcare Monitoring System designed to support astronauts during their life in space by performing daily physiological analyses using NASA sensor devices. The system processes these sensor results to identify clinical warnings and generates an interactive training plan—complete with real-time performance monitoring and automated rep counting—alongside a nutrition plan and a daily medical report. Additionally, the health monitor displays a full body analysis, step-by-step guides on how to take accurate measurements in 0g, and an anatomical heatmap highlighting affected body regions. It also provides guided instructions for performing eye and heart ultrasounds as well as ECG scans, allowing astronauts to capture diagnostic frames with attached clinical notes. Furthermore, the platform tracks the astronaut's active mission and the effect of mission conditions on their training sessions. Finally, it features an emergency response system with a voice agent that delivers step-by-step instructions to help an astronaut save a crewmate's life.
details:
Astropital

PROJECT OVERVIEW

Our platform keeps astronauts safe and self-sufficient on long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars. Deep-space crews face up to a 20-minute one-way communication delay with Earth, and astronauts are not medical doctors. So the platform:

- Monitors physiological telemetry continuously

- Detects early health drift against each astronaut's own personal baseline

- Prescribes gravity-adapted exercise and nutrition countermeasures

- Verifies exercise form with computer vision

- Guides crewmates hands-free through medical emergencies

HOW IT WORKS: END-TO-END ARCHITECTURE

1. Multi-Sensor Telemetry & Mission Environment Ingestion

The platform collects daily readings and habitat data, then adapts to the mission environment.

- Daily physiological and behavioral readings: resting heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, core temperature, sleep duration and mood

- Habitat sensor data: cabin CO₂ levels and radiation dose rates

- Browser Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT): a 30-second test that measures reaction time and cognitive fatigue

- Daily compliance log: morning vitals, resistive bone-loading minutes and ration intake

- Mission environments: Space Station, Deep Spacecraft, Lunar Base, or Mars Base/Rover. The system calculates light-speed communication delay (t = d / c) and switches between Live Ground Support and Autonomous Deep-Space Mode

2. Three-Layer Deterministic Health Assessment Engine

Rather than relying on black-box AI for medical scoring, our Python status engine evaluates every indicator with three transparent mathematical methods. Alerts appear on an interactive 2D four-region body heat map: Head/Neuro, Chest/Cardio, Spine/Bone, and Systemic/Immune.

1. Clinical safety thresholds. Immediately flags acute danger when a reading breaches a hard physiological bound (value > threshold high, or value < threshold low).

2. Personal anchor baseline (Z-score). Locks in each astronaut's first 7 mission days as their individual normal (mean μ and floored standard deviation σ_eff), then computes Z = (value − μ) / σ_eff.

- 2.5 ≤ |Z| < 3.0 triggers a Yellow caution, with a single-spike "Re-measure to confirm" prompt to catch sensor glitches

- |Z| ≥ 3.0 across consecutive readings triggers a Red alert

3. 7-day linear regression drift detection. Fits an Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) trend line across the trailing 7 days of readings to measure gradual slope. Even if a vital has not crossed an acute limit yet, a steep cumulative drift (drift Z ≥ 2.5) flags early deterioration before a crisis occurs.

3. Grounded AI Countermeasure & Nutrition Planner (Zero Hallucination)

When the assessment engine detects drift or elevated hazard exposure (such as space radiation, bone density loss, or headward fluid shift), it passes a structured telemetry summary to Gemini 3.6 Flash.

- Locked down: the LLM is strictly constrained by a JSON schema and grounded in our curated NASA HRP countermeasure menu (exercise_menu.json)

- Gravity-aware: it selects only exercises valid for the spacecraft's current gravity (0g in transit, 0.16g on the Moon, 0.38g on Mars), along with targeted calorie and micronutrient adjustments

- Closed-loop resource math: a deterministic module calculates the exact life-support trade-off for the workout plan: extra kcal, water consumption in mL, and CO₂ output in grams

4. Real-Time Computer Vision Form & Rep Tracking (OpenCV + MediaPipe)

To make sure astronauts perform prescribed countermeasures safely in low gravity, each exercise includes an integrated OpenCV + MediaPipe pose-estimation tracker. Using the device camera, it:

- Detects body landmarks in real time

- Counts completed repetitions automatically

- Gives instant posture feedback on whether the movement is being done properly

5. Autonomous Voice Emergency Triage ("Jarvis" via Ultravox + n8n)

If an astronaut enters a critical Red emergency state (such as acute chest pain or collapse during a Mars communication blackout), clicking the emergency alert triggers an automated n8n workflow that launches Jarvis, a real-time conversational AI voice assistant powered by Ultravox.

- Grounded in a deterministic emergency triage state machine (triage_protocol.json)

- Reads exact step-by-step clinical response instructions aloud

- Guides the crewmate through vitals checks and stabilization without improvising medical dosages

- Packages a Store-and-Forward Telemetry Packet, stamped with estimated Earth arrival time, for Flight Surgeons

6. Flight Surgeon PDF Mission Health Report

With one click, astronauts or crew medical officers can export a formatted PDF Mission Health Report for mission records or ground review. It summarizes:

- 14-day vital trends

- Personal baseline comparisons

- Active countermeasure plans

- Life-support resource estimates

- Emergency logs

MISSION-CRITICAL BENEFITS FOR DEEP-SPACE ASTRONAUTS

1. High-ROI mission protection and a dual-use business model. Deep-space seats cost tens of millions of dollars with strict weight and life-support limits, making it impossible to send a dedicated specialist doctor for every medical field. Our lightweight software turns any astronaut into an autonomous Crew Medical Officer, protecting multi-billion-dollar missions from costly medical aborts, while scaling commercially as a dual-use B2G/B2B SaaS platform licensed to space agencies and commercial space stations.

2. Earth-independent emergency survival. On missions to Mars, one-way communication delays reach up to 20 minutes (40 minutes round trip), making real-time guidance from Flight Surgeons impossible. Our deterministic Jarvis voice triage assistant (Ultravox + n8n) empowers non-physician crewmates to stabilize acute medical emergencies hands-free using verified clinical protocols.

3. Early detection before symptoms escalate. By anchoring every vital to the astronaut's personal first-7-day baseline (Z-score) and running 7-day linear regression drift detection, the system catches slow physiological decline, such as subtle cardiovascular deconditioning, sleep erosion, or immune reactivation, days before it becomes a mission-threatening crisis.

4. Zero-hallucination, gravity-adapted countermeasures. Constraining Gemini 3.6 Flash to a verified NASA Human Research Program (HRP) countermeasure menu ensures astronauts never receive unsafe or impossible advice, automatically tailoring workouts to 0g transit (for example, treadmill-free Zero T2 regimens) versus 0.38g Martian gravity.

5. Closed-loop habitat resource protection. Every recommended exercise session calculates exact metabolic trade-offs (extra calories, water consumption, and CO₂ generation), protecting scarce spacecraft life-support reserves on multi-year missions without resupply.

6. Injury-free exercise and sensor-glitch filtering. Real-time OpenCV + MediaPipe pose tracking prevents musculoskeletal injuries during resistive loading, while single-spike "Re-measure to confirm" checks prevent false alarms caused by faulty sensors.

WHAT ARE THE IMPACTS OF THIS PROJECT?

Enabling Safe Deep-Space Exploration Beyond Low Earth Orbit

- Bridging the 20-minute Mars communication gap. As human spaceflight expands from the International Space Station to Artemis lunar bases and multi-year Mars missions, crews lose real-time guidance from Flight Surgeons on Earth and cannot evacuate in an emergency. By pairing deterministic physiological monitoring with Jarvis (our Ultravox + n8n voice triage assistant), our platform transforms autonomous medical response from a mission bottleneck into a reliable onboard capability.

- Protecting multi-billion-dollar missions and crew seat capacity. Every seat on a deep-space spacecraft carries tens of millions of dollars in cost and strict mass, volume, and life-support limits. Rather than requiring a dedicated specialist physician for every medical discipline, our software turns any astronaut into an effective Crew Medical Officer, preventing costly medical mission aborts while protecting limited water, oxygen, and calorie reserves through closed-loop resource tracking.

- Preventing silent long-duration deconditioning. Microgravity, space radiation, and isolation degrade bone density, cardiovascular fitness, vision (SANS), and immune resilience gradually over months. Catching slow 7-day baseline drift early, and verifying exercise posture with OpenCV + MediaPipe, keeps astronauts physically and cognitively mission-ready for high-stakes planetary surface operations.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Coding Languages & Core Frameworks

- Java

- Python

- TypeScript

- Angular

- Spring Boot

- FastAPI

AI & Voice Integration

- Gemini 3.6 Flash

- Ultravox

- n8n

HOW IS THE PROJECT CREATIVE?

1. Personalized anchor baselines over static hospital limits. Instead of comparing astronauts to generic medical charts, our system dynamically anchors every health reading to that specific individual's first 7 mission days using Z-scores and 7-day linear regression drift. It detects slow health decline before a crisis hits.

2. Offline-first autonomous voice triage ("Jarvis"). When a Mars communication blackout blocks real-time contact with Earth during an emergency, our integration of Ultravox and n8n provides hands-free, step-by-step clinical voice guidance using deterministic protocols (triage_protocol.json), turning any crewmate into an expert medical responder.

3. Computer vision as a personal coach. When astronauts perform daily resistive exercises (such as squats, deadlifts, or upper-body pulls) to prevent muscle atrophy and bone density loss in microgravity, maintaining proper posture is critical to avoid injury. Our platform uses a real-time computer vision module (OpenCV + MediaPipe) running locally on the device camera to act as an automated fitness coach.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

1. Distance from Earth

- A signal to Mars takes up to about 22 minutes each way, so everything has to work on board, even with no connection.

2. Emergencies on their own

- Our emergency mode is autonomous. The voice assistant talks the crew through 18 fixed triage steps, hands-free, and reports to Earth are stored and sent when the link allows.

3. NASA's real hazards

- We based our health rules on NASA's Human Research Program hazards (radiation, isolation, distance, gravity and hostile environments). Each one is tied to something we measure and a countermeasure.

4. Each astronaut's own baseline

- We compare each person to their own first week instead of a generic average.

5. Fewer false alarms

- A trend-based red alert needs two readings in a row.

6. Safe use of AI

- The AI never invents numbers. Our Java code does all the math and limits the results.

7. Doctor-only items

- Medical items like cuff settings or fluid amounts are left to a flight surgeon.

8. Limited supplies

- Food, water and CO₂ are limited on a mission, so every exercise plan shows what it costs in resources.

9. Different places

- We planned for deep spacecraft, the Moon and Mars gravity.
